Title: Rome in World Time, Part 9: Tetrarchs, Constantine, and the Christian Empire (AD 284–395)

Summary: Diocletian ended the chaos by splitting power among four emperors; Constantine fought his way to sole rule, became the first Christian emperor and built a new Rome on the Bosporus. The fourth century also saw usurpers in Britain and Gaul, the pagan emperor Julian, a Gothic victory at Adrianople that killed an emperor, and the final division of the empire in 395. At the same time, China lost its northern heartland to steppe peoples, the Gupta Empire rose in India, Aksum and Armenia became Christian, and Teotihuacan took over the Maya city of Tikal.

---

The fourth century is when Rome became recognisably "late antique": an empire run by a court and a huge bureaucracy, with emperors who wore jewelled robes and rarely visited Rome, and a state religion that changed from the old gods to Christianity in a single lifetime.

## Diocletian and the Tetrarchy (284–305)

**Diocletian**, a soldier from Dalmatia, decided the empire was too big for one man.

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 285 | Diocletian beats Carinus, the last of Carus' family, at the Margus river (Carinus is killed by his own officers) |
| 285–286 | **Maximian** becomes co-emperor in the West; crushes the **Bagaudae**, rural rebels in Gaul |
| **286–293** | **Carausius**, a naval commander, declares himself emperor in **Britain** and northern Gaul and holds out for seven years |
| **293** | The **Tetrarchy**: two senior emperors (Augusti), Diocletian and Maximian, and two juniors (Caesars), **Galerius** and **Constantius Chlorus**. Carausius is murdered by his finance minister **Allectus** |
| 296 | Constantius retakes Britain |
| 297–298 | **Revolt in Egypt** under Domitius Domitianus and Achilleus; Diocletian besieges Alexandria for eight months |
| 298–299 | Galerius crushes the Persian king Narseh; the **Peace of Nisibis** gives Rome land beyond the Tigris |
| 301 | **Edict on Maximum Prices** tries, and fails, to stop inflation by law |
| **303–311** | The **Great Persecution**, the last and harshest persecution of Christians |
| 305 | Diocletian and Maximian **abdicate**, the first emperors to retire voluntarily. Diocletian goes to grow cabbages in his palace at Split |

## Constantine (306–337)

The system broke down almost immediately, because the sons of emperors expected to inherit.

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 25 Jul 306 | Constantius dies at **York**; his troops proclaim his son **Constantine** |
| Oct 306 | In Rome, the Praetorians proclaim **Maxentius**, Maximian's son |
| 308 | At a conference at Carnuntum there are briefly six claimants to the title of Augustus |
| 310 | Maximian revolts against Constantine and dies |
| 311 | Galerius issues an **edict of toleration** for Christians just before his death |
| **28 Oct 312** | **Battle of the Milvian Bridge**: Constantine defeats Maxentius outside Rome after, he later said, seeing a sign in the sky and being told "by this sign, conquer." He disbands the Praetorian Guard |
| **313** | The so-called **Edict of Milan**: Constantine and **Licinius** grant freedom of religion and return Christian property |
| 316/317 | First war between Constantine and Licinius |
| **324** | Constantine defeats Licinius at Adrianople and **Chrysopolis**. One emperor again |
| **325** | **Council of Nicaea**: about 300 bishops condemn Arius and produce the Nicene Creed |
| 326 | Constantine has his son **Crispus** and his wife **Fausta** killed, for reasons never explained |
| **11 May 330** | **Constantinople** is dedicated on the site of Byzantium |
| 332 | Treaty with the Goths after a Roman victory |
| 337 | Constantine is baptised on his deathbed and dies (22 May) |

## Constantine's sons and the usurpers (337–363)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 337 | Soldiers in Constantinople **massacre** most of Constantine's male relatives, leaving his three sons (Constantine II, Constantius II, Constans) |
| 340 | Constantine II dies invading his brother Constans' territory |
| **350** | **Magnentius**, an army officer, is proclaimed in Gaul; Constans is killed. On the Danube, the old general **Vetranio** is proclaimed and then talked out of it by Constantius |
| **351** | **Mursa**: Constantius beats Magnentius in one of the bloodiest battles of the century |
| 353 | Magnentius kills himself |
| 355 | **Silvanus**, a Frankish general, is pushed into revolt at Cologne by court intrigue and is murdered after 28 days |
| 357 | Constantius' cousin **Julian** crushes the Alamanni at **Strasbourg** |
| 359 | Shapur II takes **Amida** after a 73-day siege; the historian Ammianus Marcellinus escapes from it |
| **360** | Julian's troops in Paris **mutiny** when ordered east and proclaim him Augustus |
| 361 | Constantius dies before they fight; Julian becomes sole emperor |
| 361–363 | **Julian the Apostate** tries to restore the old gods and restrict Christian teachers |
| 363 | Julian invades Persia and is killed in battle (26 June). **Jovian** gives up Nisibis and five provinces to get the army home |

## Valentinian, Valens and Adrianople (364–378)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 364 | **Valentinian I** (West) and his brother **Valens** (East) |
| **365–366** | **Procopius**, a relative of Julian, seizes Constantinople and is proclaimed emperor; defeated and executed |
| 21 Jul 365 | A huge earthquake near **Crete** sends a tsunami that hits Alexandria |
| **367** | The **"Great Conspiracy"**: Picts, Scots, Saxons and Attacotti attack Britain together while Roman garrisons desert; the elder Theodosius restores order |
| **372–375** | **Firmus**, a Moorish prince, revolts in Africa |
| 375 | Valentinian dies of a stroke while shouting at envoys of the Quadi |
| c. 370–376 | The **Huns** cross the Volga, crush the Alans, and push the Greuthungi Goths |
| 376 | Tens of thousands of **Tervingi Goths** under Fritigern are allowed to cross the Danube as refugees. Corrupt officials starve them; they revolt |
| **9 Aug 378** | **Battle of Adrianople**: the Goths destroy the eastern Roman army; **Valens is killed**. Ammianus compares it to Cannae |

## Theodosius (379–395)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 379 | **Theodosius I** made emperor in the East |
| 380 | **Edict of Thessalonica** makes Nicene Christianity the state religion |
| 381 | Council of Constantinople |
| 382 | Treaty settles the Goths inside the empire as allied units under their own leaders |
| **383** | **Magnus Maximus**, commander in Britain, is proclaimed by his troops, crosses to Gaul and kills the western emperor **Gratian** |
| 384 | Debate over the **Altar of Victory** in the Senate house: the pagan Symmachus against Bishop Ambrose |
| 387 | **Riot of the Statues** in Antioch over taxes; statues of the emperor are pulled down |
| 388 | Theodosius beats and executes Magnus Maximus |
| 390 | **Massacre of Thessalonica** (thousands killed in the circus after a riot); Ambrose makes Theodosius do penance |
| 391–392 | Laws ban pagan sacrifice; the **Serapeum** of Alexandria is destroyed |
| 392 | Western emperor Valentinian II is found hanged; the Frankish general **Arbogast** makes **Eugenius** emperor, with pagan support |
| **394** | **Battle of the Frigidus**: Theodosius wins, aided by a fierce wind (the bora). Thousands of his Gothic allies die, as some contemporaries noted with satisfaction |
| 17 Jan 395 | Theodosius dies in Milan. The empire is divided between his sons **Arcadius** (East) and **Honorius** (West). It is never ruled by one emperor again |

## Meanwhile, around the world

| Date | Where | What happened | Rome at that moment |
|---|---|---|---|
| 291–306 | China | **War of the Eight Princes** destroys the Jin dynasty from within | Tetrarchy |
| 292 | Guatemala | **Tikal** Stela 29: the earliest dated monument in the Maya lowlands | Tetrarchy just formed |
| 301 or 314 (disputed) | Armenia | King **Tiridates III** converts; Armenia is often called the first Christian state | Great Persecution |
| 304 | China | Xiongnu leader Liu Yuan founds a state: start of the **Sixteen Kingdoms** | Great Persecution |
| 309–379 | Iran | **Shapur II**, crowned before birth (according to legend), reigns 70 years | Constantine to Valens |
| **311** | China | **Disaster of Yongjia**: Xiongnu forces sack **Luoyang** and capture the Jin emperor | **Galerius' edict of toleration** |
| 316–317 | China | Chang'an falls; the Jin court flees south and refounds itself at Jiankang (Nanjing) | Constantine vs Licinius |
| c. 319/320 | India | **Chandragupta I** founds the **Gupta Empire** (Gupta era starts 320) | Constantine about to build Constantinople |
| c. 330s | Ethiopia | King **Ezana** of Aksum converts to Christianity under Frumentius; crosses appear on Aksumite coins | **Constantinople founded; Constantine baptised** |
| c. 335/350–375 | India | **Samudragupta** expands the Gupta Empire across northern India | Constantius II |
| 340s | Iran | Shapur II begins persecuting Christians, now seen as Rome's allies | Constantius II |
| c. 350 | Sudan | Aksum attacks the old kingdom of Meroë | Magnentius |
| 353 | China | **Wang Xizhi** writes the *Lanting Preface*, the most famous work of Chinese calligraphy | Magnentius dies |
| c. 350s–380s | Danube | Bishop **Ulfilas** translates the Bible into Gothic | Julian, Valens |
| 372 | Korea | Buddhism reaches Goguryeo | Firmus' revolt |
| c. 375 | India | Chandragupta II takes the Gupta throne (Kalidasa may have worked at his court) | Valentinian dies |
| **Jan 378** | Guatemala | A Teotihuacan-linked warlord, **Siyaj K'ak'**, arrives at **Tikal**; the king Chak Tok Ich'aak dies the same day and a new dynasty is installed | **Seven months before Adrianople** |
| **383** | China | **Battle of the Fei River**: a much smaller southern Jin army routs Former Qin, keeping south China independent | **Magnus Maximus usurps** |
| 386 | China | The Tuoba found the **Northern Wei** | Augustine converts in Milan |
| 391 | Korea | **Gwanggaeto the Great** begins expanding Goguryeo | Serapeum destroyed |
| 4th c. | Japan | The Yamato state builds giant keyhole-shaped burial mounds | |

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Northern China fell to steppe peoples before Rome did.** In 311 Xiongnu forces sacked Luoyang and captured the emperor; in 316 they took Chang'an. The Chinese court fled south to Nanjing. Rome's equivalent, the Visigoths sacking Rome, happened a century later in 410. Historians have long compared the two collapses.

**Tikal's "Entrada" and Adrianople: the same year.** In January 378 armed newcomers connected to the great city of Teotihuacan arrived at Tikal, and the local king died that day. A new dynasty followed. Seven months later Goths killed a Roman emperor at Adrianople. Both are moments where outsiders reshaped an established civilisation.

**Christian kings in Africa and the Caucasus at the same time as Constantine.** Ezana of Aksum, Tiridates of Armenia and King Mirian of Iberia (Georgia) all converted within roughly a generation of Constantine. Christianity was becoming a royal religion across a wide arc, not only in Rome.

**The Gupta "Golden Age" began as Constantinople was founded.** The Gupta era starts in 320, and Constantinople was dedicated in 330. India was entering the period associated with Kalidasa's plays, Aryabhata's mathematics (a century later) and the classic Gupta art style.

**Two "decisive" battles five years apart.** At Adrianople (378) a migrating people broke a Roman army. At the Fei River (383) a southern Chinese army stopped a northern empire that wanted to conquer all of China. One opened the door; the other closed it.

## What comes next

Part 10: Alaric sacks Rome, Britain is abandoned, the Vandals take Africa, Attila invades Gaul and Italy, and Odoacer sends the last western emperor into retirement. Meanwhile the Northern Wei unify northern China, the Guptas fight off the Huns, and Armenians fight Persia in the same year as the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains.

## Sources and notes

- Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* (Diocletian to Constantine, a Christian eyewitness).
- Eusebius, *Life of Constantine* and *Church History*.
- Ammianus Marcellinus, *Res Gestae*, Books 14–31 (353–378). One of the best Roman historians, and an eyewitness to Amida and Julian's campaign.
- Zosimus, *New History*, Books 2–4.
- *Panegyrici Latini* (speeches praising the tetrarchs and Constantine).
- *Jin Shu* (Book of Jin) for China; the Allahabad pillar inscription for Samudragupta; Ezana's inscriptions at Aksum.
- Simon Martin and Nikolai Grube, *Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens* (2nd ed., 2008), for Tikal.
- Overview: [Tetrarchy (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrarchy), [Battle of Adrianople (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Adrianople), [Siyaj K'ak' (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siyaj_K%27ak%27).

**Flags:** The "Edict of Milan" was really a letter by Licinius, and the details of Constantine's vision differ between Lactantius and Eusebius. The date of Armenia's conversion is debated (301 traditional, 314 favoured by many scholars). Gupta reign dates are approximate. The interpretation of the Tikal "Entrada" (conquest, alliance or something else) is debated. Kalidasa's dates are uncertain.
